title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 206
paragraphs: But Croesus the Lydian, being present and finding fault with this opinion, declared an opinion opposite to that which had been set forth, saying as follows: “O king, I told you before also that since Zeus had given me over to you, I would avert according to my power whatever occasion of falling I might see coming near your house; and now my sufferings, which have been bitter, have proved to be lessons of wisdom to me. If you suppose that you are immortal and that you command an army which is also immortal, it will be of no use for me to declare to you my judgment. But if you have perceived that you are a mortal man yourself and command others who are so likewise, then learn this first: that for the affairs of men there is a revolving wheel, and that this in its revolution does not suffer the same persons always to have good fortune. I therefore now have an opinion about the matter laid before us which is opposite to that of these men. For if we shall consent to receive the enemy into our land, there is for you this danger in so doing: if you are worsted, you will lose in addition all your realm, for it is evident that if the Massagetai are victors, they will not turn back and flee, but will march upon the provinces of your realm. On the other hand, if you are the victor, you will not be victor so fully as if you should overcome the Massagetai after crossing over into their land and should pursue them when they fled. For against what I said before, I will set the same here again, and say that you, when you have conquered, will march straight against the realm of Tomyris. Moreover, besides what has been said, it is a disgrace and not to be endured that Cyrus the son of Cambyses should yield to a woman and so withdraw from her land. Now therefore it seems good to me that we should cross over and go forward from the crossing as far as they go in their retreat, and endeavor to get the better of them by doing as follows. The Massagetai, as I am informed, are without experience of Persian good things, and have never enjoyed any great luxuries. Cut up therefore cattle without stint, dress the meat, and set out for these men a banquet in our camp; moreover, provide without stint bowls of unmixed wine and provisions of every kind. Having done this, leave behind the most worthless part of your army, and let the rest begin to retreat from the camp toward the river. For if I am not mistaken in my judgment, when they see a quantity of good things, they will fall to the feast, and after that it remains for us to display great deeds.”
